issues.legal_issue: A later title-and-possession suit is barred by res judicata, even though the earlier suit sought eviction on a tenancy basis, when the same tenancy-derived status was directly and substantially litigated and a finding of adverse possession became final against the relevant defendants.
material_facts: The earlier suit sought rent and possession, relying both on a rent note and on the alleged tenancy of the defendants’ father under the owner’s predecessor.
The trial court rejected the tenancy claims and found that the defendants had acquired title by adverse possession.
The plaintiff’s appeal was dismissed as time-barred against two defendants, and the adverse-possession finding concerning them was not disturbed in the later appeals.
The later suit involved the same parties and property, sought title and possession, and again relied on the alleged tenancy of the defendants’ father.
issues.conclusion: The later suit was barred by res judicata against the two defendants for whom the adverse-possession finding had become final, but not against the other defendants.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a matter directly and substantially in issue that has been finally adjudicated between the same parties concerning the same subject matter cannot be reopened in a subsequent suit. A difference in the form of relief or in the later suit’s emphasis on title does not avoid the bar where the tenancy-derived status was directly and substantially in issue and its rejection was necessary to the earlier adverse-possession finding. The Court relied on Krishna Behari Roy v. Banwari Lall Roy for the rule against retrying a finally determined issue concerning status.

rule.if: prior_eviction_proceeding and later_title_and_possession_proceeding and same_parties_and_property and tenancy_derived_status_directly_litigated and adverse_possession_finding_left_final_for_those_parties

predicates.prior_eviction_proceeding: A claimant brought an earlier proceeding seeking possession by evicting occupants on a tenancy basis.
predicates.later_title_and_possession_proceeding: The claimant later brought a proceeding seeking a declaration of title and possession of the same property.
predicates.same_parties_and_property: The earlier and later proceedings involved the same opposing parties and the same property.
predicates.tenancy_derived_status_directly_litigate: The parties directly disputed whether the occupants’ status derived from an earlier tenancy of their predecessor.
predicates.adverse_possession_finding_left_final_fo: A court found that the occupants had acquired title by adverse possession, and that finding remained undisturbed and final as to those parties.

issues.definition: When the same parties litigate the same property in an earlier eviction proceeding and a later title-and-possession proceeding, the later suit is barred as to parties against whom a directly litigated tenancy-derived status and an adverse-possession finding became final.

issues.legal_issue: A trial-court finding can become final against defendants who were not reached by an appeal because the appeal against them was dismissed as untimely, even when the appeal proceeded against other defendants.
material_facts: The trial court found that the defendants had acquired title by adverse possession.
The plaintiff’s appeal against two defendants was dismissed as time-barred, while the appeal against other defendants was considered on its merits.
Neither the later appellate decision nor the High Court’s decision disturbed the trial court’s finding as to the two defendants whose appeal was dismissed as time-barred.
The plaintiff did not obtain a further appellate decision disturbing that finding.
issues.conclusion: The trial court’s adverse-possession finding became final between the plaintiff and the two defendants whose appeal was dismissed as time-barred; the appeal concerning the other defendants did not unsettle that finality.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the requirement of final adjudication under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It relied on Sheosagar Singh v. Sitaram Singh, which recognized that a decision may support res judicata where there was no appeal in law against it, and considered Ashgar Ali Khan v. Ganesh Dass in addressing when an issue has been finally decided.

predicates.earlier_suit_with_multiple_defendants: A claimant brought an earlier suit against multiple defendants.
predicates.appeal_against_some_defendants_dismissed: The claimant’s appeal against some defendants was dismissed because it was filed too late.
predicates.trial_finding_left_undisturbed_for_those: The trial court made a finding concerning those defendants, and no later appellate decision altered it as to them.

issues.definition: When an earlier suit involved multiple defendants and an untimely appeal left a trial-court finding undisturbed as to some of them, that finding is final between the parties as to those defendants.

issues.legal_issue: A party may raise res judicata for the first time in the Supreme Court when the prior decision had not become final while connected appeals were being heard together, but became final after no further appeal was pursued.
material_facts: Second appeals arising from the earlier and later suits were heard together by the High Court and disposed of by a common judgment.
The plea of res judicata was not raised at that hearing.
The issue concerning adverse possession became final after the High Court’s decision in the earlier suit was not taken further by the claimant.
The defendants raised the plea of res judicata in the Supreme Court appeal from the later suit.
issues.conclusion: The defendants could raise the plea of res judicata for the first time in the Supreme Court after the relevant issue had become final.
issues.legal_principle: A plea based on res judicata ordinarily cannot be invoked in connected appeals before the earlier decision is final for purposes of the later suit. The Court applied the finality principles discussed in Sheosagar Singh v. Sitaram Singh and Ashgar Ali Khan v. Ganesh Dass.

predicates.appeals_from_related_suits_heard_togethe: Appeals arising from an earlier suit and a later suit were heard together and disposed of together.
predicates.prior_issue_not_final_during_joint_heari: The decision on the relevant issue in the earlier suit had not yet become final when the connected appeals were heard together.
predicates.prior_decision_became_final_after_no_fur: The decision on the relevant issue later became final because no further appeal was pursued against it.
predicates.later_appeal_before_supreme_court: An appeal concerning the later suit came before the Supreme Court.

issues.definition: When related appeals are heard together before the earlier decision is final, and that decision becomes final afterward without a further appeal, the res judicata plea may be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court appeal concerning the later suit.

issues.legal_issue: A final adverse-possession finding against some defendants does not bar a partial decree against them where their interests are separate and distinguishable from those of the other defendants.
material_facts: Two defendants were minors in the earlier suit and their interests were represented by another defendant.
The Court regarded the minors’ interests as separate and distinguishable from the individual interests of the other defendants.
The earlier suit had produced a decree against another defendant on that defendant’s own account, and the claim concerning a separate portion of the property had been abandoned in the later suit.
issues.conclusion: A decree for partial possession could be made against the defendants whose adverse-possession title was final, without creating inconsistent decrees; the objection based on the possibility of inconsistent decrees did not apply.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that a minor’s interest remains separate and distinguishable from the individual interest of a person who represents the minor. Given that separation and the history of the claims concerning the property, a partial possession decree was possible and the principle concerning abatement and inconsistent decrees did not apply.

predicates.possession_proceeding_with_multiple_defe: A proceeding seeking possession involved multiple defendants.
predicates.represented_minors_have_separate_interes: Minor defendants were represented by another defendant, but their interests were separate and distinguishable from that representative’s individual interests.
predicates.claim_confined_to_part_of_property_or_di: The relief sought could be limited to a distinct portion of the property or to defendants with distinct interests.

issues.definition: When a possession proceeding involves multiple defendants, represented minors have separate interests, and the claim can be confined to a distinct portion or defendants, a partial possession decree is permitted without inconsistent decrees.
